stages.title: Computational chemistry
stages.hook: Experiments on a new drug molecule can take months. Could a computer predict its shape, energy and reactivity first, and how far can we trust it?
explain: Computational chemistry solves approximations of the Schrödinger equation. The Born–Oppenheimer approximation treats the heavy nuclei as fixed while electrons adjust, giving a potential energy surface E(R). Hartree–Fock (HF) treats each electron in the average field of the others and misses electron correlation. Post-HF methods (MP2, CCSD(T)) add correlation, and density functional theory (DFT) uses the electron density with an approximate exchange–correlation functional.

Accuracy costs time. A basis set is the set of functions used to build orbitals; larger sets are more accurate but costlier. Formal scaling with the number of basis functions N is about N⁴ for HF, N³–N⁴ for typical DFT, N⁵ for MP2 and N⁷ for CCSD(T). By the variational principle, the energy from a trial wavefunction is never below the true ground-state energy.

Geometry optimisation seeks a stationary point where forces vanish. A minimum has all real vibrational frequencies and a transition state has exactly one imaginary frequency. Energies come in hartree: 1 Eh = 27.21 eV = 2625.5 kJ/mol. Results must be validated against experiment or higher-level benchmarks, since errors differ by method.

example.q: A conformer energy gap is 0.020 Eh. Express it in kJ/mol (1 Eh = 2625.5 kJ/mol).
steps: A difference this large favours the lower conformer overwhelmingly at room temperature.

stages.title: Quantum chemistry
stages.hook: Why do hydrogen atoms emit light only at particular colours, and why does a molecule like O₂ hold together while He₂ does not?
explain: Quantum chemistry describes electrons by wavefunctions ψ, with |ψ|² the probability density. The time-independent Schrödinger equation Ĥψ = Eψ gives quantised energies. For a particle in a one-dimensional box of length L, Eₙ = n²h² ÷ (8mL²), so energy rises as n² and falls as the box widens.

For the hydrogen atom, Eₙ = −13.6 eV ÷ n². A transition from n = 3 to n = 2 releases 13.6 × (1/4 − 1/9) = 1.89 eV, a photon of λ = 1240 ÷ 1.89 ≈ 656 nm (the red Balmer line). Orbitals (s, p, d, f) are characterised by quantum numbers n, l and mₗ; electrons fill them according to the Aufbau principle, the Pauli exclusion principle and Hund's rule.

Molecular orbital theory builds MOs from atomic orbitals: bonding MOs lower energy, antibonding raise it. Bond order = (bonding electrons − antibonding electrons) ÷ 2. For N₂ the value is 3, for O₂ it is 2 with two unpaired electrons (paramagnetism), and for He₂ it is 0, so no stable molecule.

example.q: Compute the photon energy for the n = 2 → n = 1 transition in hydrogen (Eₙ = −13.6/n² eV).

stages.title: Advanced materials thermodynamics
stages.hook: Why do some alloys mix completely while others separate on cooling, and why does every real crystal contain missing atoms?
explain: For an ideal solution of components A and B with mole fractions x and 1 − x, the entropy of mixing is ΔSmix = −R[x ln x + (1 − x) ln(1 − x)] and ΔGmix = RT[x ln x + (1 − x) ln(1 − x)]. At x = 0.5 and 1000 K, ΔGmix = 8.314 × 1000 × (ln 0.5) = −5763 J/mol. Mixing is always favourable for an ideal solution.

Real alloys have an enthalpy of mixing. In the regular solution model ΔHmix = Ωx(1 − x). If Ω is positive, a miscibility gap opens below a critical temperature Tc = Ω ÷ 2R. For Ω = 20 kJ/mol, Tc ≈ 1203 K. Below Tc the free-energy curve has two minima and the alloy separates into two phases, which is also the basis for precipitation hardening.

Defects are thermodynamically stable above 0 K because they raise entropy. The equilibrium vacancy fraction is n/N = exp(−Q ÷ kT), with k = 8.617 × 10⁻⁵ eV/K. For Q = 1.0 eV at 1000 K, n/N ≈ 9.1 × 10⁻⁶. Chemical potential μᵢ = (∂G/∂nᵢ) drives diffusion and phase equilibrium: at equilibrium μ of each component is equal in all coexisting phases.

example.q: Find ΔGmix for x = 0.5 at 1000 K (R = 8.314 J/mol/K, ln 0.5 = −0.693).
steps: ΔGmix = RT[x ln x + (1 − x) ln(1 − x)].

stages.title: Materials modelling and simulation
stages.hook: A turbine blade must survive years of heat and stress. No single computer model covers everything from atoms to the whole blade. How do engineers cope?
explain: Modelling covers many length and time scales. Quantum methods (DFT) handle electrons for a few hundred atoms over femtoseconds. Molecular dynamics (MD) integrates Newton's laws for millions of atoms using interatomic potentials, with time steps of about 1–2 fs, so a 2 ns run with a 2 fs step needs 10⁶ steps. Monte Carlo (MC) samples configurations using the Metropolis rule: accept a move with probability min[1, exp(−ΔE/kT)].

At larger scales, phase-field and kinetic Monte Carlo describe microstructure evolution, crystal plasticity models describe grains and the finite element method (FEM) solves continuum equations for stress and heat in real components. Multiscale modelling passes information upward, such as elastic constants from DFT into FEM.

Diffusion can be extracted from MD through the mean squared displacement (MSD): in three dimensions MSD = 6Dt. Machine-learned interatomic potentials trained on DFT data offer near-DFT accuracy at much lower cost, but only within their training domain. Any model must be verified (solving the equations correctly) and validated (matching reality).

example.q: A Metropolis move raises the energy by 0.050 eV at 300 K (kT = 0.02585 eV). What is the acceptance probability?

stages.title: Functional and smart materials
stages.hook: A spectacle frame bent flat springs back to shape when warmed. How can a material remember and respond?
explain: Smart materials change a property in response to a stimulus. Shape memory alloys such as nickel–titanium (nitinol) switch between a low-temperature martensite phase, easily deformed, and a high-temperature austenite phase. Heating drives the reversal to the original shape. Superelasticity lets nitinol recover several percent of strain when the load is removed.

Piezoelectric materials like PZT ceramics and quartz generate charge when stressed and change shape when a voltage is applied. The direct effect is Q = d₃₃F, and the strain is S = d₃₃E for field E. With d₃₃ = 400 pC/N, a force of 10 N gives 4 nC. Piezoelectrics are used in sensors, ultrasound and precision positioners. They require a crystal structure without a centre of symmetry.

Other functional materials include ferroelectrics (switchable polarisation), magnetostrictive alloys, photochromic and thermochromic dyes, electrochromic windows and self-healing polymers with embedded capsules or reversible bonds. Magnetic materials lose their ferromagnetism above the Curie temperature. Design uses the coupling between mechanical, thermal, electrical, magnetic and optical properties.

stages.title: Advanced composites
stages.hook: Modern airliners are about half composite by weight. How do you design a material whose strength depends on direction?
explain: Fibre-reinforced polymers use stiff, strong fibres (carbon, glass, aramid) in a polymer matrix. They are anisotropic. Along the fibres the rule of mixtures gives E₁ = VfEf + VmEm, and across them the inverse rule 1/E₂ = Vf/Ef + Vm/Em. For 60% carbon fibre (230 GPa) in epoxy (3 GPa): E₁ ≈ 139 GPa but E₂ = 1 ÷ (0.6/230 + 0.4/3) ≈ 7.4 GPa.

Laminates stack plies at chosen angles, for example [0/±45/90]s. A quasi-isotropic layup has nearly equal in-plane stiffness in all directions. Classical lamination theory predicts laminate stiffness from ply properties. Load transfer between fibre and matrix occurs through shear at the interface, with critical fibre length lc = σf·d ÷ (2τ): for σf = 3000 MPa, d = 7 µm and τ = 30 MPa, lc = 350 µm.

Failure modes include fibre breakage, matrix cracking, fibre–matrix debonding and delamination between plies. Delamination is a particular concern after impact. Ceramic-matrix composites (e.g. SiC/SiC) serve in hot engine parts, and metal-matrix composites add stiffness to light alloys. Manufacturing methods include autoclave curing, resin transfer moulding and automated fibre placement. Recycling thermoset composites remains a challenge.

stages.title: Surface engineering
stages.hook: A drop of water beads up on a lotus leaf but spreads on glass. Many failures start at a surface. Can we change only the outer micrometres to make a part last?
explain: Surfaces decide wetting, friction, wear, corrosion and fatigue life. Young's equation gives the contact angle of a liquid drop: cosθ = (γSV − γSL) ÷ γLV, where the γ values are surface energies. For γSV = 50, γSL = 20 and γLV = 72.8 mN/m, cosθ = 0.41, so θ ≈ 66°, a partly wetting surface. A contact angle above 90° is hydrophobic.

Archard's wear law is V = K F s ÷ H, where V is worn volume, K a wear coefficient, F load, s sliding distance and H hardness. Increasing hardness reduces wear. For K = 10⁻⁴, F = 10 N, s = 1000 m and H = 10⁹ Pa, V = 10⁻⁹ m³, which is 1 mm³.

Techniques include PVD and CVD thin films (TiN, DLC), anodising of aluminium, nitriding and carburising steels, thermal spray coatings and shot peening, which introduces compressive residual stress that slows fatigue cracks. In Langmuir adsorption, coverage θ = KP ÷ (1 + KP), important for catalysis and corrosion inhibitors. Coatings must adhere well and match thermal expansion to the substrate.

teach.topic: Why surfaces matter and how we engineer them
teach.model: Wear, corrosion, wetting and fatigue start at the surface, so changing only the outer layer can improve a whole part. Coatings, hardening treatments and peening are common tools, but adhesion and thermal match are essential.

stages.title: Biomaterials
stages.hook: A hip implant must survive millions of steps inside a warm, salty, chemically active body for decades. What does a material need to be accepted and to last?
explain: A biomaterial interacts with biological systems for a medical purpose. Biocompatibility means an appropriate host response in a specific application, not a universal property. Metals used include titanium alloys (Ti-6Al-4V), cobalt–chromium and stainless steel; polymers include UHMWPE for joint bearings, silicones and PLA; ceramics include alumina, zirconia and hydroxyapatite Ca₁₀(PO₄)₆(OH)₂, whose Ca/P ratio is 10/6 ≈ 1.67 and resembles bone mineral.

Mechanical match matters. Bone has a modulus of roughly 10–30 GPa, while titanium alloy is about 110 GPa and CoCr about 210 GPa. If an implant and bone deform together (equal strain), the load fraction carried by the implant is E_iA_i ÷ (E_iA_i + E_bA_b). A stiff implant carries more load and the bone, under-loaded, may resorb, called stress shielding.

Degradable polymers like PLA and PLGA break down by hydrolysis of ester bonds and are used in sutures and scaffolds. Proteins adsorb to a surface within seconds, shaping the cellular response; surface chemistry and topography matter. Corrosion releases ions, wear generates debris and sterilisation must not damage the material. Regulation and clinical trials ensure safety.

example.q: An implant (E = 110 GPa, area 1.0 cm²) sits parallel to bone (E = 20 GPa, area 4.0 cm²) under equal strain. What fraction of load does the implant carry?

analogies.tech: A phone case shields electronics; a coating shields an implant from body fluids.

stages.title: Integrated materials discovery and design
stages.hook: Finding the right material used to take decades of trial and error. How can data, theory and experiments be combined to find one faster?
explain: Design starts from function. Ashby's method turns requirements into a performance index to rank materials. For a light, stiff beam of fixed length and loading, minimise mass by maximising E^½ ÷ ρ. For a light stiff tie it is E ÷ ρ, and for a stiff plate E^⅓ ÷ ρ. With E in GPa and ρ in g/cm³, steel (200, 7.85) gives √200 ÷ 7.85 = 1.80, and aluminium (70, 2.7) gives 3.10, so aluminium makes a lighter beam of the same stiffness.

Discovery pipelines combine high-throughput computation (DFT databases), CALPHAD thermodynamic modelling, machine-learning screening and targeted experiments. A funnel narrows candidates: from 10 000 candidates, a 5% pass of a DFT screen leaves 500, and if 10% of those pass experiments, 50 remain. Models need cross-validation to detect overfitting, uncertainty estimates and data in standard, open formats. Autonomous labs and Bayesian optimisation choose the next experiment to learn the most.

Real design balances many objectives: stiffness, strength, cost, processing, supply, recyclability and life-cycle environmental impact, assessed with life-cycle assessment (LCA). Trade-offs have no single best answer, and Pareto-optimal sets show the best compromises. Ethical choices include sourcing of critical minerals, toxicity and end-of-life design for circularity.

example.q: Compare steel and aluminium for a light stiff beam using E^½ ÷ ρ (steel E = 200 GPa, ρ = 7.85 g/cm³; Al E = 70 GPa, ρ = 2.7 g/cm³).
